title: Change tracking versus AsNoTracking (read vs write paths)
hook: By default EF Core watches every entity you load — ready to detect changes for SaveChanges. Read-only API endpoints should call AsNoTracking to skip that overhead and avoid stale tracked graphs.

blocks.text: Change tracking is EF Core's identity map — it remembers loaded entities, compares current values to originals, and generates UPDATE statements on SaveChangesAsync. AsNoTracking() tells EF Core not to track query results — lower memory use, faster materialization, no risk of accidental updates. Use tracking for write paths (load entity, modify, SaveChanges). Use AsNoTracking for read-only GET endpoints, reports, and projections to DTOs. AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution() deduplicates entities in graph results without full tracking overhead.

entries.plainDefinition: In-memory snapshot of loaded entities and their state (Added, Modified, Deleted, Unchanged).
Query hint that returns detached entities EF will not monitor for changes.
Entity not associated with any DbContext tracker — changes are ignored by SaveChanges.
entries.example: Returning tracked entity from API without AsNoTracking can cause surprise updates.

entries.plainDefinition: AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution ensures same row maps to one object in a graph query.
entries.example: Include with AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution avoids duplicate Customer instances.

blocks.text: List endpoints that return thousands of rows with tracking enabled allocate identity maps and snapshots — measurable CPU and memory cost at scale. Tracked entities returned from a long-lived scope (or accidentally cached) can write stale data on a later SaveChanges. Senior interviewers ask: when do you use AsNoTracking? What breaks if you use it on an update flow? How does tracking interact with Include and concurrency tokens?

blocks.title: Default in EF Core 7+ for read queries
blocks.body: You can set QueryTrackingBehavior.NoTracking as default and opt into tracking for writes with .AsTracking(). Many API projects configure NoTracking globally and explicitly track only mutation endpoints.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Query executes
items.body: SQL returns rows from the database.

items.title: Materialization
items.body: EF creates entity objects. With tracking, each is registered in the change tracker with original values snapshot.

items.title: Read-only response
items.body: AsNoTracking: entities are detached, serialized to JSON, garbage collected after response.

items.title: Write path contrast
items.body: Tracked entity: property change sets Modified state; SaveChangesAsync emits UPDATE for changed columns only.

diagram.title: Change tracker in a Web API
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph read["GET /api/orders"]
    Q1[AsNoTracking query] --> D1[Detached entities]
    D1 --> JSON[JSON response]
  end
  subgraph write["PUT /api/orders/id"]
    Q2[Tracked query or Attach] --> T1[Change tracker]
    T1 --> MOD[Property changed\nState = Modified]
    MOD --> SAVE[SaveChangesAsync\nUPDATE SQL]
  end

snippet.label: Global NoTracking with explicit tracking for writes
snippet.explanation: NoTracking default suits read-heavy APIs. AsTracking() on mutation paths ensures SaveChanges detects modifications. Clear convention: reads never call AsTracking unless needed.

snippet.label: Projection avoids tracking entirely
snippet.code:
var summaries = await db.Orders
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Pending)
    .Select(o => new OrderSummaryDto(
        o.Id,
        o.Total,
        o.Customer.Name)) // join translated to SQL
    .ToListAsync(ct);
snippet.explanation: Select to DTO never tracks — EF materializes only DTO columns. Preferred for list endpoints: less memory than full entities even with AsNoTracking.

snippet.label: Update patterns: tracked load vs Attach
snippet.explanation: Pattern A is clearest for server-owned updates. Pattern B avoids SELECT but risks overwriting columns if IsModified is too broad. Never Attach after AsNoTracking load of a different instance with same key.

snippet.label: Diagnostics — memory and query tags
snippet.explanation: TagWith links SQL to route in logs. Tracked-entities counter rising on GET endpoints signals missing AsNoTracking. Compare GC metrics in load tests to prove production impact.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using AsNoTracking then trying to SaveChanges on those entities — changes ignored. Loading tracked entities for GET list endpoints — memory bloat. Attach entire client-sent entity marking all properties modified — overwrites columns. Mixing tracked and no-tracking instances with same key in one context — InvalidOperationException.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: load test a list endpoint before/after AsNoTracking — measure p95 latency and Gen2 GC collections. EF Core logged SQL is identical; savings are in materialization and tracker overhead. dotnet-counters tracked-entities during GET-only workload should stay near zero with correct config. Application Insights dependency duration may drop slightly; bigger win is memory under high RPS.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Must AsTracking or Attach for updates
More mapping code; best SQL shape

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying AsNoTracking 'disables the database' — it only skips the identity map. Not knowing tracked entities can cause accidental SaveChanges updates. Claiming tracking is always free — it has real memory cost at scale. Unable to explain Attach vs load-then-modify.

interviewTakeaways: Change tracking watches loaded entities for SaveChanges; AsNoTracking returns detached entities for read-only paths.
When not to use AsNoTracking: update flows needing Modified detection, or when you rely on fix-up for Includes before save.
Production tip: default NoTracking for read-heavy APIs; use Select projection; monitor tracked-entities counter on GET load tests.

60s: Tracking builds identity map for SaveChanges. Read APIs use AsNoTracking or project to DTO. Writes use AsTracking or Attach. Global NoTracking default with explicit tracking on mutations is a common production pattern.
Follow-up: how does AsNoTracking interact with optimistic concurrency RowVersion?
commonPitfalls: AsNoTracking on update then wondering why SaveChanges does nothing — detached entities are invisible to the tracker.
Returning 10k tracked entities from a list endpoint — memory and GC pressure under load.
Strong answer: 'Reads: AsNoTracking or Select to DTO. Writes: tracked load or targeted Attach. I set NoTracking default globally and prove impact with load tests and tracked-entities counter.'
introducedIn: EF Core 1.0; QueryTrackingBehavior default config in EF Core 5+

jsTsCorrelations.note: Prisma has no change tracker — every update is explicit prisma.order.update(). EF developers coming from Prisma should consciously choose tracking vs AsNoTracking instead of assuming implicit dirty checking.
TypeORM tracks entities like EF Core. find() tracks; getRawMany() does not. Same read/write split applies — use query builder with no entity hydration for read-only Express routes.
